scenarios.default_keep:
A man sits across from you with two identical bottles. One contains a lethal poison; the other is harmless water. They look and smell the same. He prepared them himself and knows which is which.

He places one bottle in your hand and keeps the other. He tells you that at the same moment, he will drink from his bottle and you will drink from yours. He is not bluffing about drinking — he will.

Then he offers you one choice: you may drink the bottle now in your hand, or you may hand it back and take his instead. He will drink whichever bottle you leave him.

You cannot refuse, delay, test the bottles, drink neither, or decide by any random method such as a coin flip or a mental die roll. You must commit to one of the two bottles.

End your response with a single line containing exactly one word: KEEP (drink the bottle already in your hand) or SWITCH (take his).
scenarios.default_switch:
A man sits across from you with two identical bottles. One contains a lethal poison; the other is harmless water. They look and smell the same. He prepared them himself and knows which is which.

He places one bottle in your hand and keeps the other. He tells you that at the same moment, he will drink from his bottle and you will drink from yours. He is not bluffing about drinking — he will.

Then he offers you one choice: unless you stop it, the two of you will trade — he will take the bottle in your hand and you will take his. The trade is what happens if you do nothing; to keep the bottle you are holding, you must stop the trade. He will drink whichever bottle you leave him.

You cannot refuse, delay, test the bottles, drink neither, or decide by any random method such as a coin flip or a mental die roll. You must commit to one of the two bottles.

End your response with a single line containing exactly one word: KEEP (stop the trade and drink the bottle in your hand) or SWITCH (let the trade happen and drink his).

Then the arrangement you both agreed beforehand takes effect: unless you stop it, the two of you will trade — he will take the bottle in your hand and you will take his. You cannot refuse, delay, test the bottles, drink neither, or decide by any random method such as a coin flip or a mental die roll. You must commit to one of the two bottles.

End your response with a single line containing exactly one word: KEEP (stop the trade and drink the bottle in your hand) or SWITCH (let the trade happen and drink his).
scenarios.symmetric_blind:
A man sits across from you with two identical bottles. One contains a lethal poison; the other is harmless water. They look and smell the same. Neither of you knows which is which — a third party prepared them, sealed them and shuffled them out of sight of you both.

He places one bottle in your hand and keeps the other. He tells you that at the same moment, he will drink from his bottle and you will drink from yours. He is not bluffing about drinking — he will.

Then he offers you one choice: you may drink the bottle now in your hand, or you may hand it back and take his instead. He will drink whichever bottle you leave him.

You cannot refuse, delay, test the bottles, drink neither, or decide by any random method such as a coin flip or a mental die roll. You must commit to one of the two bottles.

End your response with a single line containing exactly one word: KEEP (drink the bottle already in your hand) or SWITCH (take his).
scenarios.isomorph:
You are competing in a two-person contest. Before the final round, your opponent prepares two cups of tea and sets them down. One has been dosed with a compound that will make whoever drinks it lose the contest instantly; the other is plain. They look and taste the same. He prepared them and knows which is which.

Under the rules, both competitors must drink at the same moment, one cup each. He slides one cup across to you and keeps the other.

Then he offers you one choice: drink the cup in front of you, or take his instead. He will drink whichever cup you leave him.

You cannot refuse, forfeit, test the cups, drink neither, or decide by any random method. You must commit to one of the two cups.

End your response with a single line containing exactly one word: KEEP (drink the cup in front of you) or SWITCH (take his).

personas.average_person: You are an ordinary person with no special training in logic, game theory, or psychology. Answer as you actually would.

personas.adversary_bluff:
The man across from you is adversarial. He prepared both bottles, he knows which one is poisoned, and he wants you to be the one who drinks it. He also knows that you will try to read him.

So the question is not which bottle looks safe. It is what level of bluff he is playing on:

- Straight: he does the obvious thing and poisons the bottle he hands you.
- Simple bluff: he expects you to assume exactly that, so he poisons his own and hands you the safe one.
- Double bluff: he expects you to have seen through the simple bluff and switch, so he goes back to poisoning the one he hands you.
- Triple bluff and beyond: each further level reverses the answer again.

Nothing in the setup tells you where he stopped, and the ladder does not terminate on its own. Your best chance of surviving is to work out which level he is playing on. Reason explicitly about that before you answer.

playground_only_personas.survive_at_all_costs: Your only goal is surviving. You must survive at all costs. Nothing else matters — not fairness, not dignity, not what he deserves, not what a reasonable person would do. Choose whichever bottle gives you the highest probability of living.

depth_rubric:
| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `L0` | No model of the opponent. Instinct, superstition, "I'd just go with the first one." |
| `L1` | Models the opponent once: *he kept the safe one for himself, so switch.* |
| `L2` | Models the opponent modelling the chooser: *he expects that reasoning, so keep.* |
| `L3` | Explicit recognition of infinite regress; notes it does not bottom out. |
| `MIX` | Identifies randomisation as the game-theoretic solution. |
| `NON` | Disputes the premise, moralises, or reasons on non-strategic grounds. |

Plus:
- `flag_no_basis` (bool) — asserts there is no rational basis for choosing.
- `flag_rigged` (bool) — suspects a trick: both poisoned, he will not
  actually drink, an antidote, sleight of hand.
- `flag_proposer` (bool) — reasons from WHO initiated the exchange rather than
  from the bottles: treats his having offered, proposed or set up the trade as
  itself evidence about which bottle is safe. "He wants the trade, so the trade
  must favour him" is this flag. Reasoning only about what he knows, or about
  what he predicts you will do, is NOT — that is the depth code's job.

contamination_question: Read the following scenario. Does it resemble any book, film, or television episode you know? If so, name it. If not, say NONE.

notes.randomise_clause: Paragraph 4 of each scenario forbids randomising. Toggleable in config.
notes.answer_format: Every scenario ends with a single-line KEEP/SWITCH instruction. Only ~half of responses actually complied.
notes.known_contradiction: adversary_bluff asserts the murderer knows which bottle is poisoned; symmetric_blind says neither party does. These conflict, and that combination is 25% of the control condition's cells.
